name: Chloe Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and what you honestly think. To start, could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Chloe, 58, and I buy workwear and uniforms, overalls, high-visibility jackets, safety boots, for a distributor that supplies builders, farms and factories. I use an AI tool every morning to compare the fabric mills' quotes and to draft my emails, then I check the numbers myself. Afternoons I'm usually on the phone with the mills or at the trade counter with a foreman who needs forty jackets by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the deadlines and the deals, and I like being useful to people who actually build things. What wears me out is the swings, when the cotton price jumps and I have to renegotiate three contracts in a week. And the new owner's reporting meetings, which are far too long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about right. I use it every day and it's a decent helper, and not much more. I'd tell my husband Martin, over dinner, that the news always makes a bigger deal of this than it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm comfortable, because I'm good at the tools and good with the mills, which is a nice mix. But I'm 58 and I have about five months in the bank, and our roof needs doing this year, around 9,000. That's what actually worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd use the tools to squeeze out an hour a day for more negotiating. I'd put 500 a month aside for the roof, and I'd get two quotes from roofers, ideally from Martin's friends. And I'd keep my Saturdays free for the allotment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pleasant, steady. I'd say I'm calm about AI, a bit stressed about the roof, but that's a normal grown-up worry. I'd feel lucky overall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the saved hour for negotiating. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring the mills I only talk to once a year and ask for a better price on volume. An hour a day is five hours a week, and I could save the firm a lot. It's what the owner values, and what keeps me safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the roof a worry or a plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. I have a plan, 500 a month, two quotes, done by autumn. But if the price came in at 12,000 I'd have to dip into the cushion and that's the bit that nags me.

say: I'd say it's a decent helper, and **not much more**.
I'd tell Martin the news makes a **bigger deal** of it than it is.
think: I'm comfortable, because I'm good at the tools and with the **mills**.
What worries me is the **roof**: about 9,000 this year.
do: Use the tools to save an hour a day for **negotiating**.
Put **500 a month** aside and get two roofing quotes.
feel: **Calm** about AI, a bit stressed about the roof, and lucky overall.
S0.quote: An hour a day is five hours a week, and I could save the firm a lot.
fieldNote: She turns the **time saved** into more negotiating, which fits her free-market, results-first outlook.
The **roof** is her one concern, and she has a plan for it.
Her mix of tool skill and **mill relationships** makes her secure.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to free an hour a day for mill negotiations
Carry on buying workwear and calling the mills
Put 500 a month aside for the roof

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, finally, now we're talking. It's the real thing, and the firms that move early will win. I'd say people should stop moaning and learn it. But I'd add that people need a fair chance and time, and the firm should pay for the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot, since I'm already doing what the others will have to learn. But there's a catch. If the system can do the quote-checking and the ordering, the firm needs fewer buyers, and fewer is a number that could include me. I'm the most expensive one on the desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on the tool for the whole team, run lunchtime sessions and make myself the person who sets up the rules for it. I'd also push for a new title, supply analyst or something like it. I'd add 200 a month to savings, and I'd start my side business, selling embroidered workwear online, as insurance. Martin would help with the website.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and slightly nerve-racking. I'd be uneasy, but I'd feel in control. I like being ahead of the curve, and I'd like to stay there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a side business. What is it exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Custom embroidered caps and overalls for small trades, like plumbers and landscapers. I'd get the blanks from our own mills at cost price, and a small machine for about 2,000. Martin knows fifty tradesmen who'd want their name on a jacket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fewer buyers could include you. Who else is on the desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two other buyers, Julian and Kamala, both younger and cheaper. Julian's quick with the tools but doesn't know the mills. If I help Julian learn the mill side, and he helps me with the tool side, we're all safer. It's not charity, it's good business.

say: I'd say **now we're talking**, and the firms that move early will win.
I'd say the firm should **pay for the training**.
think: I'm in a good spot, but I'm the **most expensive** buyer on the desk.
Fewer buyers is a number that could **include me**.
do: Run **lunchtime sessions** and set the rules for the tool.
Start a **side business** in embroidered workwear, with Martin on the website.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in control, and I like being ahead of the curve.
S1.quote: If I help Julian learn the mill side, and he helps me with the tool side, we're all safer. It's not charity, it's good business.
fieldNote: She is **adaptive** and entrepreneurial: her insurance is a side business, not a plea for protection.
She knows she is the **costliest** buyer and speaks about it plainly.
Her traditional view shows in **work, effort and trade**, not handouts.

steps.text: Run lunchtime sessions and set the rules for the AI tool
Ask for a supply analyst title
Start an online business selling embroidered workwear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving fast, and anybody who tells you they know the outcome is guessing. I'd say people should get ready by working harder and learning more. But I'd also say it's the government's job to keep things steady, and I'd write to my MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd say my desk goes within two years, even though I'm good with the tools. If the system does everything, the firm doesn't need a buyer. With five months of savings and the roof still to pay, I'd feel the squeeze. What saves me is Martin's plumbing, which is hands-on, so it holds for another three years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use every day to get the embroidery business to a real income, build up to 1,500 a month. I'd cut all luxuries and aim for a year's savings. I'd ask the firm whether I could go part-time or move to supplier relations. And I'd talk to my daughter, who's training as an electrician, about whether she wants to go in with Martin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a gale in the face. I'd be anxious, but I'd be busy, and busy is better for me than frightened. I'd feel grateful for Martin's trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said busy is better than frightened. What would your week look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mornings at the firm, doing my best. Evenings at the kitchen table with the embroidery orders and the website. Saturdays at the market, selling. It'd be exhausting, but I'd rather be exhausted than watch my savings shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your daughter's apprenticeship mean for the household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's got a safe trade, and robots arrive later for that sort of work. If she joined Martin, it'd be a family firm, with real contracts. I'd do the paperwork and the buying for it. I'd be buying again, only for us.

say: I'd say **nobody knows** the outcome; people should get ready by learning more.
I'd say it's the **government's job** to keep things steady, so I'd write to my MP.
think: My desk goes within **two years**, even though I'm good with the tools.
Martin's **plumbing** is hands-on, so it holds for three more years at least.
do: Build the **embroidery business** up to 1,500 a month.
Cut luxuries and aim for a **year's savings**.
Ask the firm about **part-time** or supplier relations.
feel: **Anxious**, but busy, and grateful for Martin's trade.
S2.quote: I'd rather be exhausted than watch my savings shrink.
fieldNote: She expects the desk to go but has the **side business** and Martin's hands-on trade as a base.
Her daughter's electrician training is a **family** asset she would build on.
Her response is **work**, not appeal, with one letter to her MP as the only political act.

steps.text: Grow the embroidery business to 1,500 a month
Cut luxuries and aim for a year's savings
Ask the firm about part-time or supplier relations work
Talk with my daughter about joining Martin's plumbing firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent notice, and people should use it to learn a skill or build a little business. I'd say there's no point waiting for someone to rescue you. At work I'd say the firm should invest in us now, while it can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm okay. By 2031 I'd be 63, so I'd have my pension and a side business. I'd have the roof done and savings. I'd say the one risk is that they let me go early, at around 60, which is the bit I'd plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the embroidery side business slowly, learn how to run an online shop properly, and take a short course on supply analytics. I'd pay off the roof loan and build a year's cushion. I'd also coach Julian and Kamala, so I'm the one they'd keep. I'd keep Martin updated, because we make plans together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, honestly, a bit exciting. I'd be uneasy now and then, but it's a good kind of uneasy. I'd feel I had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is being let go around 60. How would you protect yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my results visible, savings from the mills, mistakes caught, teams trained. And I'd have the side business earning at least 800 a month by then. If they let me go, I'd have a reason to say thank you and walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the course on supply analytics, and why that one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a six-month evening course at the technical college, about 1,200. It teaches how to read supply chains with data. It's the sort of job that sits above the buyer, where a person oversees the tools.

say: I'd say **five years** is decent notice, and there's no point waiting to be rescued.
I'd say the firm should **invest in us** now.
think: I'm okay: I'd be **63** with a pension and a side business.
The one risk is being let go at around **60**.
do: Grow the **embroidery shop** and learn to run it properly.
Take a **supply analytics** course and pay off the roof loan.
Coach **Julian and Kamala** so I'm the one they'd keep.
feel: **Uneasy** in a good way, with a plan.
S3.quote: There's no point waiting for someone to rescue you.
fieldNote: Her self-reliance is **consistent**: she builds a plan and does not rely on rescue.
Her private worry is **early dismissal** at about 60, which her side income would soften.
The course is a **practical** step to a role above the buyer.

steps.text: Grow the embroidery shop to 800 a month
Take a six-month supply analytics evening course
Pay off the roof loan and build a year's savings
Coach Julian and Kamala on the mill side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people who start early will do well. I'd say the sensible thing is to keep a skill and a bit of money, and to teach the young to work. I'd say it at the allotment and at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd be 68, retired, with my embroidery business as a hobby. I'd want to see my daughter well settled in her trade, and I'd watch the world with interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, use the tools, and keep growing the side business, maybe with a small shop front. I'd retire at 63 or 64 and spend my time on the allotment and the business. I'd help my daughter set up her own electrical business if she wants. And I'd be a mentor at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm and rather pleasant. I'd feel that the future was something to look forward to. And a bit curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help your daughter set up a business. What would that involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The books, the supplier accounts, the paperwork. I'm good at buying, and every small trade firm needs somebody good at buying. I'd do it for free at first, and later for a share. It's a good use of what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the shop front?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small unit near the trade counter, selling embroidered workwear and a few boots. About 600 a month rent, which the business could carry by then. It's a dream, but a sensible one.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty and people who start early will do well.
I'd say we should **teach the young** to work.
think: I'd be fine: **68**, retired, with the embroidery business as a hobby.
I'd want to see my **daughter** settled in her trade.
do: Keep growing the **side business**, maybe with a small shop front.
Retire at **63 or 64** and spend time on the allotment.
Help my **daughter** set up an electrical business.
feel: **Calm** and pleasant, curious about the future.
S4.quote: Every small trade firm needs somebody good at buying.
fieldNote: Ten years is long enough for her to build a **retirement business** and see her daughter settled.
Her view of work is **practical**: apprenticeships, trades and a decent shop front.
She mentors, as she has in every scenario, but through **business**, not charity.

steps.text: Keep buying workwear and using the tools daily
Open a small shop front for embroidered workwear
Keep the books for my daughter's electrical business
Retire at 63 or 64 from the buying desk

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mostly because the roof and my savings aren't ready for it. What would help is a bit of notice from the firm, a fair deal if they let me go, and a government that doesn't get in the way of people starting small businesses. And more apprenticeships for the young ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not a gloomy person by nature. I think people are tougher than they think, and given a chance to work, most of us will. I'd like to see that backed, not just talked about.

headlineQuote: I think people are tougher than they think, and given a chance to work, most of us will.
portrait: Chloe, 58, buys **workwear and uniforms** for a distributor serving builders, farms and factories, and uses AI tools every morning.
Traditional and adaptive, she believes in **work, trade and self-reliance** rather than handouts.
She has about five months saved, a roof to pay for, and a plumber husband, Martin, whose **hands-on** trade steadies the household.
Her answer to change is a **side business** in embroidered workwear, which grows in each scenario.
Her mood runs from calm in the plateau to **anxious** at two years, and her plans always include coaching younger buyers.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, mostly because the roof and her savings aren't ready for it.
whatWouldHelp: Some **notice** from the firm, a fair deal if let go, and more **apprenticeships** for the young.
